What's with the Whales?

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What mystery, lurking beneath the waves, is driving whales from the depths and into near-certain death on land? We look into what science is telling us about an increase in whale beachings.

Unique Selling Point:
Recent research suggests there's been a 15% increase in whale stranding in the past few years in the U.K. A mixture of scientific study and anecdotal evidence tells us that is probably true of other parts of the world. It's something that mystifies the people dedicating their lives to preserving these remarkable creatures, although theories abound: climate change, naval activity, sonar, wind farms... there are as many possible explanations as there are whales. We head to sea to talk to experts about which of these - if any - are most likely.

Summary:
Of all nature’s unanswered questions, whale beaching is among the most curious and unsettling. Just last week, seven Northern Bottlenose Dolphins died on a popular beach in the west of Ireland despite the best efforts of locals to keep them alive (footage available). At almost the same time, another pod was beaching in the Faroe Islands, although locals there were less inclined to save them.

South Africans, too, have seen this tragic phenomenon at first hand: in an incident that made global headlines in 2009, 50 Pilot Whales beached themselves at Kommetjie in the Western Cape. 20 were saved.
https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/31/science/earth/31whales.html

A report last year suggested Cetacean beaching had increased by 15% in a six-year period, with 5000 whales and dolphins stranded around the UK between 2011 and 2017. The question is: why?

Well, research has yet to provide a satisfactory answer. There are many theories including sonar interference from offshore wind farms, naval weapons testing, blasting by the oil and gas industry, and a myriad other. Each is plausible, but none can be blamed with any conviction.
What scientists know for certain is that something is driving these creatures from the ocean depths and - given their precarious numbers – we can’t afford to lose them in these sorts of numbers. Not when fishing nets are claiming their victims, too.

This will be an insert filmed largely with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group. We will venture offshore in search of Minke whales and Humpbacks, talking to experts about the beaching scourge and what might be causing it. We will also link up with South African experts who, despite being thousands of km away, share similar concerns to the hardy Irish braving the worst of the Atlantic’s notorious weather to deepen our understanding of whales and - hopefully – figure out why they’re dying.

We will also talk to the UK Cetacean Strandings Investigation Programme, the compilers of the study.


Extra Budget Items:
Possible one night accommodation County Clare, Ireland - weather dependent.

Script:


VO: Ireland has a 3100km coastline. Its western shores look out on the wild Atlantic. 30 years ago, these waters were declared a sanctuary for cetaceans, what you and I know as whales and dolphins. 15sec

VO: Today, it’s windy with a heavy swell, remnants of a storm that passed through a few days earlier. I’m with the chief science officer at the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group, Dr Simon
Berrow. 12sec

John Upsound [C765] “It’s not the type of weather you normally go out in.”
Simon Berrow Upsound: “It’s not, it’s a day for staying at home… incredible what you see”
(Upsound “Whoa”)

VO: There are at least 25 whale, dolphin and porpoise species around Ireland 5sec (bang!) but today we won’t be seeing any of them. 3sec

VO: But I wasn’t in the west of Ireland to whale-watch – not specifically, anyway. 4sec

VO: A few weeks before, in mid-August, seven rare Northern Bottlenose Whales stranded in the Irish county of Donegal. 8sec

VO: Six of them died. One returned to deeper water, it’s survival uncertain. 6sec
Simon Berrow Upsound from ZIP folder “BEACH”

ITV Simon Berrow [09:09] STRAP: “Chief Scientist: IWDG” we felt there was nothing we could do about it (CUT) It was a conscious decision. We looked at the options and the best option was to do nothing and let them die, let them die with dignity.

VO: It fell to Dr Berrow and his colleagues to try and figure out what happened. Post-mortems aren’t always possible, but there are other ways of piecing together the puzzle. 9sec

ITV Simon Berrow [09:09] you're looking at (CUT) the pattern, the timing, the species, and then sharing it with colleagues elsewhere to see, is it local or more widespread? (CUT) it's almost a process of elimination.

VO: After sharing their images on social media, it became apparent that what he and his colleagues were dealing with was more than just a standard research opportunity. 10sec

ITV Simon Berrow [09:09] we immediately were told, well actually, yesterday there was a live stranding of Northern bottlenose Whales and the Faroes (CUT) And then we were told about Northern bottlenose whales being seen in the North Sea. A few days after our experience (CUT) bottlenose whales were seen off the West coast of Scotland (CUT) Then they were seen in the Netherlands. All of a sudden, our little piece of Donegal where something unusual happens is put on a broader context.

VO: At least six sightings or strandings of Northern Bottlenoses and other beaked whales in a matter of weeks. It turns out that in the late northern hemisphere summer something mysterious had happened in European waters. 13sec

VO: But what single event would be so significant as to drive beaked whales into an unfamiliar and life-threatening environment? 8sec

ITV Simon Berrow (06:25) STRAP “Chief Science Officer: IWDG” Remember these species in Ireland, they live way, way off shore from here. We'd have to go 150 miles before we found deep water that will be the habitat of bottlenose whales (CUT) These are your extreme deep divers.

VO: Speculation mounted that a very particular type of single event may have been responsible. 5sec

VO: Earlier that summer, the North American and European military alliance, NATO, conducted a large anti-submarine exercise off the coast of Iceland. 8sec
It ended in July – weeks before the beaked whales made their appearance. But enough is known about these mammals to suggest a connection: Their existence at extreme depth makes them susceptible to noise - and there’s no shortage of that when there are submarines to be hunted. 18sec

VO: Naval SONAR emits extremely loud sounds for hundreds of kms in every direction. According to several studies, its impact on whales could be significant, driving potentially life-threating behavioural changes. 15sec

VO: Could this explain what unfolded in August? 4sec
Rob Deaville [08:36] it's an unusual and atypical event. We do.... My door.... (laughs) that’s my door. Do you mind if we pause and pick up on that?

John Upsound: Sure, of course.

VO: Rob Deaville heads up the Cetacean Strandings Investigation Programme at the Zoological Society of London. The CSIP says strandings around the U.K. have increased by about 15% in the past few years. 14sec

Rob Deaville Upsound [09:30]: “Sorry mate, postmen right? Always good timing.”
John Upsound: “Laughs”

VO: He relies on a detailed, historical stranding record to determine which are part of a regular pattern, and which are anomalies. What happened in August was the latter. 11sec

ITV Rob Deaville (09:32) I personally never dealt with anything this unusual with a number of live strandings of beaked whales and mixed species too.

VO: The challenge is figuring out whether what caused it was natural or – as was speculated – unnatural. 7sec

ITV Rob Deaville [26:10]: STRAP “Zoological Society of London” you don't need to be a rocket scientist to look out there and see that we're living in a changing world. And those changes will inevitably have impacts on mobile Marine species, like cetaceans (CUT) Now we need to work out what those impacts are and what, if anything we can do to improve or reduce those.

VO: That’s easier said than done, so pinning it down to a single cause like a naval exercise is plausible but not conclusive. 8sec

ITV Rob Deaville [02:05] if you look at a few of the causes (CUT) that are directly manmade, things like fishing, gear, bycatch, ship strike, you know, you can see direct evidence of that on the body you're examining, and that's fairly clear (CUT) things like exposure to marine pollution, chemical pollution, or noise, or impacts from climate change. That's a little harder to directly determine.

Simon Elwen Upsound:

VO: 10 000 km away, Dr Simon Elwen is on the lookout for whales off the False Bay coast. He’s a specialist in marine mammal ecology. 9sec

Simon Elwen Upsound:

VO: Despite picking up evidence of their presence, not even friendlier seas than those encountered in Ireland a few days before can guarantee a sighting. 10sec

VO: With his years of stranding experience in South Africa and Namibia Dr Elwen is familiar with the challenge of separating the natural from the unnatural. 10sec

ITV Simon Elwen [06:12] STRAP “Director: Sea Search” Most strandings around the South African coast (CUT) are natural. Animals die. They get predated upon. They get ill. When they’re ill a lot of cetaceans choose to come in shore (CUT) and if they're ill and near shore, and there's a storm, it's quite likely that they might strand (CUT) but increasingly in both South African, especially in European and American waters, there's been a large increase in strandings associated with human impacts.

VO: And there’s a long list of those, both direct causes such as ship strikes and entanglements and indirect impacts like offshore windfarms and oil and gas exploration. Climate change, too, is playing a significant role – driving species into unfamiliar habitats in search of food. But, when it comes to the European strandings in August, it appears the single event theory provides a credible smoking gun. 26sec

ITV Simon Elwen [21:40] what seems to happen when they’re exposed to these loud sonars is that they get a fright and they shoot to the surface much more quickly than they should. And so what seems to be happening is the animals are getting embolisms. You know, they're getting gas bubbles in their ears and in their tissues (CUT) It causes disorientation and presumably causes intensive pain.

John Question [14:30] How concerned should we be at these sorts of events and the impact they might have on beaked whales in particular?

ITV Rob Deaville [15:09] we don't really know much about them. We don't know about their population size. We don't know very much about the threats that they face, and we don't know what impact we are having on them. So (CUT) it's quite important to try and gather as much information as we can from events like these.

VO: Deaville will continue collaborating with other Cetacean researchers to do just that. Until then, he – like his colleagues – is reluctant to draw hard and fast conclusions about what happened in August. The single event theory is plausible - maybe even probable - but the science behind these strandings is nothing if not complex. Not least because, tragic as they are, these events are also crucial to science. 26sec

ITV Simon Elwen [01:10] Strandings give us a lot of information on species that we just don't encounter from, from the boat or from shore, especially deep water species like beaked whales (32:12) There's very low chance of success for refloating. So it's always, it's always a saddening event to, to see animals die (CUT) And that's why it's important for us as researchers to try and get the most we can out of those and learn the most we can from those animals in terms of what they eat and their parasite loads. And have they been impacted by humans and to engage with the right people (CUT) to be able to reduce those human impacts.

VO: For some rare beaked whale species, the stakes could not be higher. 5sec

ITV Rob Deaville [15:09] the last thing we want to do is potentially to face a situation where they disappear on our watch (CUT) we're not there necessarily yet, but I think that lack of information is something I'd be quite concerned about as a scientist. We just need to learn more about them to therefore learn more about what we might be doing to them.

VO: And that’s probably as true of our relationship with all nature, as it is of whales. 6sec

ENDS.

That's a little harder to directly determine. Simon Elwen Upsound: VO: 10 000 km away, Dr Simon Elwen is on the lookout for whales off the False Bay coast. He’s a specialist in marine mammal ecology. 9sec Simon Elwen Upsound: VO: Despite picking up evidence of their presence, not even friendlier seas than those encountered in Ireland a few days before can guarantee a sighting. 10sec VO: With his years of stranding experience in South Africa and Namibia Dr Elwen is familiar with the challenge of separating the natural from the unnatural. 10sec ITV Simon Elwen [06:12] STRAP “Director: Sea Search” Most strandings around the South African coast (CUT) are natural. Animals die. They get predated upon. They get ill. When they’re ill a lot of cetaceans choose to come in shore (CUT) and if they're ill and near shore, and there's a storm, it's quite likely that they might strand (CUT) but increasingly in both South African, especially in European and American waters, there's been a large increase in strandings associated with human impacts. VO: And there’s a long list of those, both direct causes such as ship strikes and entanglements and indirect impacts like offshore windfarms and oil and gas exploration. Climate change, too, is playing a significant role – driving species into unfamiliar habitats in search of food. But, when it comes to the European strandings in August, it appears the single event theory provides a credible smoking gun. 26sec ITV Simon Elwen [21:40] what seems to happen when they’re exposed to these loud sonars is that they get a fright and they shoot to the surface much more quickly than they should. And so what seems to be happening is the animals are getting embolisms. You know, they're getting gas bubbles in their ears and in their tissues (CUT) It causes disorientation and presumably causes intensive pain. John Question [14:30] How concerned should we be at these sorts of events and the impact they might have on beaked whales in particular? ITV Rob Deaville [15:09] we don't really know much about them. We don't know about their population size. We don't know very much about the threats that they face, and we don't know what impact we are having on them. So (CUT) it's quite important to try and gather as much information as we can from events like these. VO: Deaville will continue collaborating with other Cetacean researchers to do just that. Until then, he – like his colleagues – is reluctant to draw hard and fast conclusions about what happened in August. The single event theory is plausible - maybe even probable - but the science behind these strandings is nothing if not complex. Not least because, tragic as they are, these events are also crucial to science. 26sec ITV Simon Elwen [01:10] Strandings give us a lot of information on species that we just don't encounter from, from the boat or from shore, especially deep water species like beaked whales (32:12) There's very low chance of success for refloating. So it's always, it's always a saddening event to, to see animals die (CUT) And that's why it's important for us as researchers to try and get the most we can out of those and learn the most we can from those animals in terms of what they eat and their parasite loads. And have they been impacted by humans and to engage with the right people (CUT) to be able to reduce those human impacts. VO: For some rare beaked whale species, the stakes could not be higher. 5sec ITV Rob Deaville [15:09] the last thing we want to do is potentially to face a situation where they disappear on our watch (CUT) we're not there necessarily yet, but I think that lack of information is something I'd be quite concerned about as a scientist. We just need to learn more about them to therefore learn more about what we might be doing to them. VO: And that’s probably as true of our relationship with all nature, as it is of whales. 6sec ENDS.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): What mystery, lurking beneath the waves, is driving whales from the depths and into near-certain death on land? We look into what science is telling us about an increase in whale beachings.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Recent research suggests there's been a 15% increase in whale stranding in the past few years in the U.K. A mixture of scientific study and anecdotal evidence tells us that is probably true of other parts of the world. It's something that mystifies the people dedicating their lives to preserving these remarkable creatures, although theories abound: climate change, naval activity, sonar, wind farms... there are as many possible explanations as there are whales. We head to sea to talk to experts about which of these - if any - are most likely.
metadata.Summary: Of all nature’s unanswered questions, whale beaching is among the most curious and unsettling. Just last week, seven Northern Bottlenose Dolphins died on a popular beach in the west of Ireland despite the best efforts of locals to keep them alive (footage available). At almost the same time, another pod was beaching in the Faroe Islands, although locals there were less inclined to save them. South Africans, too, have seen this tragic phenomenon at first hand: in an incident that made global headlines in 2009, 50 Pilot Whales beached themselves at Kommetjie in the Western Cape. 20 were saved. https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/31/science/earth/31whales.html A report last year suggested Cetacean beaching had increased by 15% in a six-year period, with 5000 whales and dolphins stranded around the UK between 2011 and 2017. The question is: why? Well, research has yet to provide a satisfactory answer. There are many theories including sonar interference from offshore wind farms, naval weapons testing, blasting by the oil and gas industry, and a myriad other. Each is plausible, but none can be blamed with any conviction. What scientists know for certain is that something is driving these creatures from the ocean depths and - given their precarious numbers – we can’t afford to lose them in these sorts of numbers. Not when fishing nets are claiming their victims, too. This will be an insert filmed largely with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group. We will venture offshore in search of Minke whales and Humpbacks, talking to experts about the beaching scourge and what might be causing it. We will also link up with South African experts who, despite being thousands of km away, share similar concerns to the hardy Irish braving the worst of the Atlantic’s notorious weather to deepen our understanding of whales and - hopefully – figure out why they’re dying. We will also talk to the UK Cetacean Strandings Investigation Programme, the compilers of the study.
